Both Joseph Pratt households are linked to the tree, with 11 new `pe_` links from the 1880 record and 9 from the 1860 record (pe_001 to pe_020).

Edges: census, household record. The parent-child and couple edges (R1 to R5) already exist from the 1841 and 1851 records, so I wrote no new relationship edges.

Household check: Ann (I2), Joseph (I4) and Sarah Pratt (I3, b. ~1847) are the head's family; none has a death on file. Joseph and Ann are present in 1880. Sarah is absent in 1880, aged about 33. That is an open identity question: she may have married, died, been enumerated elsewhere, or be a different family. It needs a researcher's decision and is not resolved here.

Links, all `confident` with a 0.78 `same_person` score on every persona:
- 1860, Salt Lake County: head Joseph (I1), wife Ann (I2), daughter Sarah (I3), son Joseph (I4).
- 1880, Salt Lake County: head Joseph (I1), wife Ann (I2), son Joseph (I4). The wife and son relationship assertions also link to the head, scored on his persona.

Why `confident` despite a 0.78 score: name, age, birthplace and household composition all agree with the tree, and the children were already tied to both parents by the 1851 record. The move from Cranfield, England (1851) to Salt Lake (1860) is about 7,767 km. The Utah emigration wiki page states that many Latter-day Saint immigrants from Great Britain came on ships from Liverpool, England. I treated that as a corridor bridging the move and quoted it in each link's `move_bridge`. The sentence is generic, so a reviewer could reasonably want a passenger list or similar record before accepting the move. The 1880 links cite the 1851 Cranfield residence as the nearest pre-run residence, not the 1860 record.

Warnings: `person_warnings` reports one "nonStandardPlace" item per person (I1 to I4). These concern the existing Cranfield residence facts, not the new links. Materializing the facts added no conflicts.

Next step: proof-conclusion for q_001, which has no proof summary yet, and a researcher's decision on Sarah's absence in 1880.

The 1860 and 1880 Salt Lake County census households are now tied to Joseph Pratt, his wife Ann, and their children Sarah and Joseph in the family tree, with strong confidence. The 1851 Cranfield, England record already placed these people in the family, and the names, ages and English birthplace in both American census records agree with it. The move from England to Utah is not documented by a passenger list or similar record in the project, but a Utah emigration guide describes many English Latter-day Saint immigrants arriving by ship from Liverpool, which makes the move plausible; a researcher may still want a direct record of the crossing. Sarah, who is about 13 in 1860, does not appear in the 1880 household, and her absence is an open question: she may have married, died, or been counted somewhere else. The next step is for the conclusion stage to write the proof summary for the question of whether this is the subject's family, and a researcher should decide what became of Sarah.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

I linked all eight personas in the 1870 and 1880 Maury County households to the matching people in the tree, but every link is capped at `probable`. The records fit the family well, yet nothing on file explains how the Horsham family came to be in Tennessee.

**Links written (22 `pe_` entries, pe_001 to pe_022), all at `probable` with match score 0.78:**
- William Weller (I1): head in 1870 (src_001) and 1880 (src_002), plus both spouse and son relationship assertions.

- James Weller (I3): son, 18 in 1870.
- Ellen Weller (I4): daughter, 15 in 1870.
- George Weller (I5): son, 11 in 1870 and 21 in 1880.

Birth years agree with the 1861 Horsham household in the tree in every case, with a gap of zero years. Names, birthplace and household composition all agree.

**Why the cap:** The tree places the family in Horsham, Sussex, England in 1861. The records place them in Maury County, Tennessee, about 6,804 km away. The project holds no passenger list or naturalization record. The Tennessee emigration page names only settlers' origins and gives no arrival, so it does not supply a corridor. The move is therefore unexplained, which keeps every link at `probable`.

**Open identity questions:**
- James (b. ~1852) and Ellen (b. ~1855) are absent from the 1880 Maury household, and the tree shows no death for either. They may have died, been enumerated elsewhere, or separated.
- The move from England to Tennessee needs a passenger list, naturalization, or other bridging record before any link can rise to `confident`.

**Other actions:**
- Materialized the 1870 and 1880 facts onto I1 through I5, adding 1870 and 1880 residence facts to William. Nothing was marked primary or preferred.
- The household's parent-child and couple edges already exist from the 1861 record, so I added none.
- `person_warnings` reports only a non-standard-place notice on existing facts, with no impossible dates.

agent_returns.text:
No links were written. None of the five assertions should be attached to William Hartley (I1), and the head of the household has no tree person to attach to.

**Why I1 is not a match.** The 1881 lodger is 36 and born in Halifax, which fits I1's birth year of about 1845. But I1 already has a burial fact dated 16 February 1870, aged 25, from the Halifax St John burial register, and two confident links (pe_005, pe_006) back that burial, plus two more (pe_007, pe_008) from the cemetery register. A census taken in 1881 cannot place a man who was buried in 1870. `same_person` scored the pair at 0.52 and flagged the 1881 record as an impossible entry against that burial. Under the threshold policy, an impossible entry backed by confident links means a different person, so this is a no-link. The score does not override that.

**Per assertion:**
- **a_001 (name), a_002 (birth), a_003 (residence, Hanson Lane), a_004 (woolsorter):** not linked to I1. Each is a lodger persona of the 1881 record, and the lodger is a different William Hartley on the tree's evidence.
- **a_005 (name of Samuel Greenwood, head of household):** not linked. Samuel is not in the tree, and nothing in the project ties him to the Hartley family. A stub would be unsupported, and I did not mint one because the request did not ask for a stub.

**Next steps for the researcher:**
- Decide whether the 1870 burial is really about the same William Hartley as the 1861 son. If it is, the 1881 lodger is a namesake and the record should stay unlinked. If the burial is a different man, the existing burial links need checking. That is a conflict-resolution question, and I did not register a conflict because that section belongs to that skill.
- If the 1881 lodger is worth tracking as a separate William Hartley, hypothesis-tracking is the right place to record it.

---
The lodger William Hartley in the 1881 Halifax census is not the William Hartley in the tree, because the tree records him as buried in 1870 and the census is eleven years later, so nothing was linked. The head of the household, Samuel Greenwood, is not in the tree at all and was left unlinked. The next step is for the researcher to decide whether the 1870 burial belongs to the same man as the 1861 son, which is a question for conflict-resolution.
